Orthodox

OR-thuh-doks — ends like 'docks'; orthodox thinkers stay at the docks instead of sailing off into strange new ideas. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Orthodox is following traditional, widely accepted beliefs or practices.

Her orthodox approach to baking meant no shortcuts and no substitutions from her grandmother's recipes.

Worked Example

A doctor sees a patient with a common infection. She prescribes exactly what the medical textbooks recommend — the standard medicine at the standard dose. Any physician in the country would have done the same.

Sticking to the accepted, standard way of doing things is orthodox. Unlike 'old-fashioned,' which implies something outdated, an orthodox method is still the recognized norm today.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

traditional: following long-established customs

conventional: conforming to accepted standards

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unconventional: not conforming to accepted ways

radical: favoring extreme or complete change

Where it sits · how unquestionable the practice has become — common → orthodox → dogmatic

common vs. orthodox: Common is weaker than orthodox — a common practice is merely widespread, while an orthodox one carries the weight of official, established acceptance.

dogmatic vs. orthodox: Dogmatic is stronger than orthodox: an orthodox thinker follows accepted beliefs, but a dogmatic one rigidly insists those beliefs are beyond all question.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ortho-

prefix — ortho-: straight, correct (Greek)

root — dox-

root — dox-: opinion, belief (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Greek ortho- (correct) plus doxa (opinion) literally means 'correct opinion.' Orthodox describes beliefs and practices a community considers the right, standard ones.

Use the root in a new word: paradox

Use the root in a new word: paradox: It sounds like a paradox, but slowing down at the icy corner actually got the drivers home faster.
